newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Nobel laureate Wiesel declines to chair Swiss fund.
newsitem.headline: Nobel laureate Wiesel declines to chair Swiss fund.

text.p: Nobel laureate and human rights activist Elie Wiesel has declined to join or chair the Swiss Fund for Holocaust victims, the Swiss Foreign Ministry said on Saturday.

Wiesel, who was appointed on May 1 as international chairman of the fund, wrote to the Swiss government that he felt deeply honoured by the appointment, but he saw no possibility of taking up the position. "It was never his role to measure or quantify the suffering of others," the ministry quoted Wiesel as saying in his letter.
In New York, friends of Wiesel said the letter also contained a reference to "recent statements in the Swiss media" as deepening his reservations about serving.

The letter did not specify which statements but sources close to the World Jewish Congress, which had pressed for Wiesel's candidacy, said they were shocked that when the Swiss government announced the appointment of Wiesel as the commission's international chairman, it also said the title would carry no special powers.
Jewish groups will meet Monday in New York to name a replacement for Wiesel on the seven-member commission.

Wiesel, who survived two concentration camps and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986 for his writings and lectures dealing with the horror of the Holocaust, added he was willing to help the fund with any advice he could offer.
The Swiss Cabinet, which set up the fund in February, said it deeply regretted Wiesel's decision.

However, the government's aim is for the fund to start work as soon as possible and it has already sent a letter to Israel Singer, general secretary of the World Jewish Congress (WJC), asking for a new person to be nominated to the fund's board.

The World Jewish Restitution Organisation, an umbrella group run by the WJC, nominated Wiesel along with Josef Burg, a former Israeli minister, and Avraham Hirschson, a member of the Israeli Knesset's restitution committee, to the fund.

Wiesel's unwillingness to join the fund follows criticism by some Jewish groups, including the WJC in Brussels, of the Swiss government for allegedly dragging its feet in appointing Jewish nominees for the fund.
Rolf Bloch, head of the Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities, is to head the seven-member board of the fund, named the "Special Fund for Holocaust Victims in Need."

The decision to create the fund helped defuse the country's worst foreign policy crisis since the Second World War, sparked by allegations that Swiss banks hoarded unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and that neutral Switzerland cynically profited from the war.

The fund is separate from a proposed Solidarity Foundation that would sell official gold reserves to finance aid to victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights outrages, including the Holocaust.
